opening.headline: Let's address the issue of accessing columns that the model does not need to read, by using the authorization that extends from the data to the model.
body: In AI services handling customer data, the most common mistake is not that the model answers incorrectly, but that the model is left in a state where it can access data it doesn't need to read. Before attempting to fix the model, one must first examine who has access to which columns and rows within which tables.

In this class, we will examine Unity Catalog's approach to granting and verifying permissions, row filters and column masks that restrict query access to specific rows and columns at query time, and ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control) for consistently applying the same rules across multiple tables. Finally, we will walk through a case where certain columns of customer data are masked, and we will review the habit of setting up configurations and then reading and verifying the results.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the behavior of Unity Catalog permissions, row filters, and column masks
It is possible to distinguish whether a permission issue arises at the data, model, or serving layer.

screens.title: The model reads columns it should not read.
screens.lead: First, let's examine one scene illustrating how a data access incident occurs. Read along with the diagram and follow who is touching what.

visual.alt: A scene where a customer table is connected by arrows to a person, a service subject, and a model serving endpoint.
labels: The purchase history summary only needs the purchase amount.
Part of the resident registration number appears mixed in the response.

paragraphs: The customer table includes columns for name, phone number, resident registration number, and purchase amount. We have developed a chatbot that summarizes the purchase history based on this table. The chatbot only needs access to the purchase history, but the service account that invokes the chatbot is configured to read the entire table.

On one occasion, a partial citizen number was reported to be mixed into a chatbot response. While changing the prompt or switching models might seem like a solution, the root cause is not the model. The model itself is not responsible because the service account had permissions broader than the required scope, allowing sensitive input values—such as a partial citizen number—to be present from the start in the input that the model could access.

When addressing this issue, it is necessary to distinguish the entity performing the read operation. In cases where a human directly makes a query, when a service entity makes the query on behalf of the human, or when a model serving endpoint retrieves data, all may access the same table, but they can do so with different privileges. This course covers how permissions propagate through data, model, and serving layers.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Distinguish whether the root cause lies within the model or within the data scope provided to the model. Review why this distinction is important again when the lesson concludes.

screens.outro: Now let's think about how you're dividing access permissions in your environment.

screens.title: How are we dividing access permissions?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to type or submit your answer, so just think of it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Are you granting data access privileges only at the table level, or do you grant them down to the column and row level as well?
items.answer: Dividing tables solely by row would either block the entire table due to a single column, or conversely, require opening the entire table solely for a single column. In this course, we will discuss row filtering and column masking—methods that keep the table open but limit which rows and values are visible during querying.

items.prompt: Are the permissions for user accounts and service accounts following the same rules?
items.answer: People often grant broad permissions for their work, and service accounts are frequently assigned similar permissions for convenience. However, since service accounts repeatedly read data in places that people do not directly access, the principle of granting only the necessary scope of access becomes more important.

items.prompt: Can we immediately say who has the permission and who owns the object?
items.answer: In Unity Catalog, every secure object has an owner, and there are defined principals who can grant permissions. Knowing both the owner and the grant path allows you immediately to determine who should be checked for what when issues arise. If this is unknown, it represents an area that needs improvement.

screens.outro: Based on the current approach, let's first verify Unity Catalog's fundamental structure for handling permissions.

screens.title: Unity Catalog Permissions: Owner, GRANT, default is no access
screens.lead: When you select the image number marker, you can view detailed information. Select sequentially from number 1 to verify how permissions are assigned and inherited.

visual.alt: Diagram showing the layer tree of catalog, schema, and table under MetaStore, along with the permissions required at each layer.

markers.label: Default is access denied
markers.title: At first, nothing is open.
markers.body: In Unity Catalog, users initially do not have permission to access data in the metadata store. Access must be explicitly granted by someone. Account administrators, workspace administrators, and metadata store administrators have the basic permissions required to manage Unity Catalog. Therefore, the starting point of permission design is not what to restrict, but what to grant.

markers.label: owner
markers.title: Every object has a owner.
markers.body: Every secure object in Unity Catalog has an owner. The owner holds all permissions on that object and can grant permissions to other principals. The owner can also grant MANAGE permissions to other users, enabling them to manage the permissions of that object. Therefore, MANAGE permissions are not appropriate to grant to principals that merely read data, such as service accounts.

markers.label: Who can provide it?
markers.title: The principal who can grant authority
markers.body: Permissions can be granted to four categories: the owner of the object, the owner of the catalog or schema that contains the object, a user who has MANAGE permission on the object, and the metastore administrator. Account administrators can also directly grant permissions to the metastore. In case of issues, this list serves as contact information to determine who should be consulted.

markers.label: Three commands
markers.title: GRANT, REVOKE, SHOW GRANTS
markers.body: Permissions are granted, revoked, and queried using SQL commands. `GRANT` grants permissions to a principal, `REVOKE` revokes them, and `SHOW GRANTS` shows currently assigned permissions to who. A principal can be a user, a service principal, or a group, and a service principal is represented by an applicationId value. The same operations can also be performed using Databricks CLI, Terraform provider, or Catalog Explorer.

markers.label: Inheritance and Required Permissions
markers.title: It's important from which layer the input comes.
markers.body: Permissions are inherited from parent to child objects. Catalog-level permissions affect all schemas and tables beneath it, so granting broad permissions is convenient but inadvertently exposes many tables. To read a single table, it is generally necessary to grant `USE CATALOG` permission on the catalog, `USE SCHEMA` permission on the schema, and read permission on the table itself. Grant only the necessary permissions to service principals at the required layers.

screens.outro: Having confirmed the unit responsible for opening the object, we will now proceed to discuss methods for restricting the row and column values within the object.

screens.title: row filter, column mask, and ABAC
screens.lead: Explore the differences in filtering rows, filtering values, and consistently applying filters across multiple tables when selecting a tab.

tabs.label: row filter
tabs.body: Row filter limits the rows that a user can see. The filter is a SQL user-defined function (UDF) that is evaluated on a row-by-row basis at query time. Rows that return `FALSE` are excluded from the result set. It is commonly used in row-level security to display only records corresponding to a user's region, department, or account. A row filter applied directly to a table is set using the `ALTER TABLE SET ROW FILTER` statement and is managed by the table owner.

tabs.label: column mask
tabs.body: A column mask controls the values that users see in a specific column. A mask is a SQL user-defined function (UDF) that takes a column value as input and returns either the original value or a masked value. The return type must be compatible with the column's data type or castable to it. Only one mask can be applied to a single column, and the mask can be configured to behave differently based on various attributes. A mask set using the ALTER TABLE ALTER COLUMN SET MASK applies only to that column in the table.

tabs.label: Table Direct Setup
tabs.body: Placing directly on the table is simple and easily visible, but requires separate configuration for each table and column. As the number of tables increases, the same function must be linked multiple times, and someone might accidentally omit it when a new table is added. This approach is suitable when applying simply to a few tables or when specific exception rules are needed for certain tables.

tabs.label: ABAC Policy
tabs.body: ABAC is an access control model that uses properties expressed as governance tags to identify data that needs protection by applying policy conditions. Policies are attached to layers such as catalog, schema, or table, and automatically apply to objects that have tags. Thus, a single policy can enforce consistent rules across multiple tables, and new tables are automatically included in the protection scope as long as they are tagged. To create a policy, the user must have `MANAGE` permissions or ownership over the target object, as well as `EXECUTE` permissions for filter or mask UDFs. If consistent rules across multiple tables are required, ABAC policies are recommended.

tabs.label: Lineage
tabs.body: Lineage tracks where data originates and where it flows. Knowing which sensitive columns connect to specific tables and models, or dashboards, makes it easier to determine where policies should be applied. However, policies do not end with simply being implemented; instead, one must review the entire data flow path to ensure no gaps exist.

screens.outro: Having confirmed the concept, let's now examine actual SQL statement by statement and see what each line defines.

screens.title: SQL reading: row filter and column mask on a per-row basis
screens.lead: Read the following SQL from top to bottom. The explanation on the right describes what each line specifies and the symptoms that appear when a setting is misaligned. The condition expressions are simplified examples for ease of reading.

notes.note: The mask_ssn function accepts a STRING value and returns a STRING. If the user is a member of the compliance group, it returns the original value; otherwise, it returns a masked value. If the return type does not match the column type, an error may occur during the masking step or the value may be altered in an unintended manner.

Connect the function created earlier to the ssn column of the cust table using a mask. Only one mask can be applied to a single column, so if you want to apply a different mask to the same column, you must replace the existing mask. Without this line, the function will be created but will not hide any column, so all users will see the original data unchanged.

The region_filter function returns a BOOLEAN. Here, it returns TRUE only for rows where region is NULL. Rows for which the function returns FALSE are excluded from the result. The input parameter type must match the type of the column to be joined.

The region value is passed as a function argument. If the types differ, a conversion is involved. If a string cannot be converted, it becomes NULL when ANSI mode is off, but an error occurs when ANSI mode is on. In both cases, the intended row behavior is not achieved, so the type must be properly matched.

screens.outro: Now that you can read the grammar, let's work through a single example, covering the entire process from design to verification.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Column Masking and Misaligned Row Filter Diagnosis
screens.lead: The instructor walks through the customer data case step by step. Select the next arrow to follow the sequence of diagnosis, design, configuration reading, symptoms, root cause, correction, and verification.

steps.title: Stage 1 Diagnosis: What is being read?
steps.body: The source material confirms which columns the service provider of the purchase history summary chatbot is reading. The chatbot only requires purchase amount and purchase history, but the service provider is also reading phone number and resident registration number columns. The issue is not with the model, but with the data scope accessible to the service provider.

steps.title: Stage 2 Design: Tag and Mask Policies
steps.body: Attach a governance tag to a sensitive column, and create a column mask policy and masking UDF based on that tag. This ensures that the same rules are automatically applied to other columns in different tables that have the same tag. Grant service subjects only the necessary catalog, schema, and table permissions, without granting them MANAGE permissions.

steps.title: Step 3: Read settings: row filter read line
steps.body: Now assume row restrictions are needed, disable ANSI mode, and read the following settings with an example containing only NULL or non-numeric strings like 'KR' in the region: `CREATE FUNCTION region_filter(region INT) RETURNS BOOLEAN RETURN region IS NULL;` and `ALTER TABLE cust SET ROW FILTER region_filter ON (region);` These two lines. The function returns BOOLEAN and returns TRUE when region is NULL. The target column for filtering is region.

steps.title: Step 4 symptom: All rows are displayed
steps.body: Upon querying as the service subject, all rows up to the one with a populated region value are returned. It appears as though the filter is not being applied at all. We need to determine whether the filter is completely not applied, or if it is applied but the condition is being evaluated differently than intended.

steps.title: Step 5 Cause: Parameter Type Mismatch
steps.body: The REGION column is of type STRING, but the function parameter is declared as INT. If ANSI mode is off, as in this example, non-numeric strings such as 'KR' fail to convert to INT and become NULL, causing the `region IS NULL` condition to evaluate to TRUE, thereby allowing all rows to pass. When ANSI mode is enabled, the same conversion results in an error. Not all strings convertible to numbers become NULL.

steps.title: Step 6: Match the type
steps.body: Change the function parameter to `region STRING` to match the column type. When re-executing the same query, only rows with NULL region remain. Note that despite changing only one type, the number of returned rows has significantly changed.

steps.title: Step 7 Verification: Read and validate the results
steps.body: The same query is executed by both the human user and the service provider, and the results are compared. The resident registration number is visible only to the compliance group as the original value, and the service provider should only see the masked value. Finally, the trace is opened to verify that there are no gaps in the flow from this table all the way to the model.

steps.title: Conclusion: Policy is verified by its outcomes.
steps.body: The model was only reading values after masking and filtering had been applied. The lesson from this case is that policy creation should not end there; instead, the actual number of rows and values produced by policy application must be read and verified. Even a policy executed without errors may behave differently from its intended purpose.

screens.outro: Having organized the example, I'll once again summarize the key points to conclude.

screens.title: Core Summary: Permissions flow from data through to the model.
screens.lead: Summarizes the content covered in class into a single coherent flow. Read it slowly and distinguish which paragraph tells the story of which layer.

paragraphs: At the data layer, the starting point of permissions is no access. Permissions are granted only to the necessary layers for the required subjects, such as owners and those possessing MANAGE privileges, and the grant status is verified using GRANT, REVOKE, and SHOW GRANTS. It is important to consider inheritance and determine at which layer the permissions are assigned.

In the row and value hierarchy, a row filter determines which rows are visible, while a column mask limits column values. Both are UDFs evaluated at query time and do not alter the original data—only the results visible to the user change. When the same rules are needed across multiple tables, governance tags enable consistency through ABAC policies.

In the model and serving layer, the data read by the service entity that invokes the model or serving endpoint constitutes the input range of the model. Therefore, when authorization issues arise, it is necessary to determine whether the authorization applies to the data, the model, or the serving endpoint. Finally, the input types of filters and masking functions must match the types of the connected columns, and the policy results must be read and verified afterward.

callout.label: Go to the beginning scene
callout.text: The cause of the incident where the resident number was mixed into the response was the scope of data accessible to the service provider, not the model. The most certain approach is to block it at the input stage using mask policies and the principle of least privilege.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: We want to consistently apply the same masking rules to sensitive columns across multiple tables. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Executes the SET MASK of ALTER COLUMN directly for each table.
Apply tag-based ABAC policies to sensitive columns with governance tags.
Grant broad MANAGE permissions to the service entity to expose it directly.
Create a row filter to exclude all rows containing sensitive columns.
checks.explain: ABAC identifies protected resources through tags, and it is recommended to apply policies automatically to objects tagged so that consistent rules can be enforced across multiple tables.

wrong.0: Direct configuration per table is possible, but it requires repetition for each table and is difficult to maintain consistency.
wrong.2: Granting authority and policy management capabilities to service entities instead of to MANAGE actually weakens control.
wrong.3: Row filtering is a tool that excludes rows, while hiding column values is the role of column masking.

checks.intro: This is a problem regarding directly reading the settings from an example. The results are not recorded.
options: Row filter can be applied to only one table, so the second row is ignored.
Row filtering is not possible using ALTER TABLE and is only achievable through policies.
The function parameter changes from INT to NULL STRING, making the condition true.
If the return type is BOOLEAN, the row that returns FALSE is included in the result.
checks.explain: This issue occurs when ANSI mode is off and the region is NULL or a non-numeric string. A value that fails INT conversion becomes NULL, resulting in IS NULL being TRUE. If ANSI mode is on, an error is raised, and numeric strings can be converted to INT. Function arguments must be matched to STRING.

wrong.0: Placing a row filter directly via ALTER TABLE on a single table is possible; the issue lies with the input type of the function.
wrong.1: The SET ROW FILTER of ALTER TABLE is the official method for applying a row filter at the table level.
wrong.3: The behavior of row filter is to exclude rows that return FALSE.

glossary.def: In Unity Catalog, the objects to which permissions can be granted, such as catalog, schema, table, and model. Every securable object has an owner.
This is the permission that allows managing object permissions and creating policies on objects. The owner can grant this to other users.
An SQL UDF-based control that excludes rows from the result where FALSE is returned during row-by-row evaluation at query time.
A SQL UDF-based control that accepts a column value as input and returns either the original value or the masked value. It can be attached to only one column.
An access control model that uses properties such as governance tags as policy conditions, automatically applying policies to objects that have the tags.

misconceptions.myth: By managing the permissions granted to the model, data exposure can be prevented.
misconceptions.fact: The model must define the columns and rows of the table it reads. Because the data the service invoking the model reads is exactly the input scope of the model.

misconceptions.myth: Masking causes the original data to be lost.
misconceptions.fact: The original value remains unchanged and differs only in the value displayed to the user at the time of inquiry. The same column may appear to the user as either the original value or a hidden value, depending on the user.

misconceptions.myth: A mask can be applied directly per table, which is sufficient.
misconceptions.fact: As the number of tables increases, repetition and omissions occur. Tag-based ABAC policies are recommended when consistent rules are needed across multiple tables.

misconceptions.myth: If policies are applied, they work as intended.
misconceptions.fact: If the types differ, an implicit conversion is applied. Incorrect conversions may result in errors or NULL values depending on ANSI mode, so ensure the function argument types match the column types and verify the results.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Permissions extend from data through to the model, and the range of data that the model can read directly defines its input range.
Unity Catalog initially grants no access, and access is granted hierarchically only to the extent necessary for owners and manage owners.
Rows are filtered by row filter, and column values are constrained by column mask at query time.
Multiple tables provide consistent rules based on ABAC policies grounded in governance tags.
The input types of filter and mask functions must match the column types, and after application, the results are read and verified.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What columns and rows are included in the data my model accesses, and which ones does my model not need to read?
